I think we are in a position to do what could be a nice project, which will be of relevance and of interest to people within the high energy physics community. That is to do the following:

Formalise the Yukawa sector of the Standard Model Lagrangian, that is showing that given the SM higgs field, and fermionic fields, show that the only terms up to mass-dimension 4 are the Yukawa terms (and the Higgs potential).

The main motivation for this project is to give the first demonstration that these sorts of calculations can be done in lean. This will be of interest to people in the high-energy physics community because it's the same sort of calculations that go into effective potentials, which are quite a hot topic. It's also the sorts of calculations that go into beyond-the-standard-model theories when you add an extra particle to the standard model and you want to try and find all of the terms that are allowed under a given symmetry. I certainly think there's a paper that can be written on this topic.

If anyone wants to get involved in this let me know (if enough are interested we could use this thread to coordinate)! I've created an API map at Physlib#1419 which gives the main steps which need to be done. (Though this is not an invitation for people to point their favourite AI models at it, in an uncontrolled manner, as I think there are lots of design decisions to be made here).

Here the LinearOrder is really just a way of picking linearly independent elements, as you say above if you have a basis b := [b₁, b₂] you can use either b₁ * b₂ or b₂ * b₁ for the basis element on the second exterior power, the first comes from saying 1 < 2 and the second from 2 < 1. But you can also do this by rewriting the basis: if I instead have the basis b' := [b₂, b₁] the basis element on the second exterior power (using the usual order 1 < 2) is b₁' * b₂' = b₂ * b₁ and you recover the other basis. In a sense the order of the indexing set is distinct from the order of the basis. You would do this with docs#Module.Basis.reindex.

The way the basis of the exterior power/exterior algebra works is it takes any basis of the underlying space and builds a basis of the exterior algebra so you can swap the order of the basis elements and the basis elements of exterior algebra react accordingly. You can then write lemmas about how the reindexing impacts the resulting basis.

I have updated Physlib#1415 with a way of approaching this without having to refer to a basis. Thinking about it a bit, I think this might be the best approach because it seems like not relying on a basis actually gives you slightly nicer constructions. The idea is to replace, for example, coefficients with respect to a basis with linear projections. For example 

def coeff (s : Multiset FieldSpecification) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential :=
ExteriorAlgebra.liftAlternating (coeffOfVectorTuple s)

Defines the projection onto the terms which have individual components specified by the multi-set s. I've also defined the support of a V : EffectivePotential to be those multi-sets for which this coefficient is zero. You can then write, although I haven't proved yet: 

lemma eq_sum_support_coeff (V : EffectivePotential) : V = ∑ s ∈ support V, coeff s V := by
  sorry

One of the nice things about this is that it generalizes for different types of "coefficient". For example, you can define the projection onto the subspace spanned by terms with given irreducible representations in it by 

def irrepCoeff (i : Multiset Irrep) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential where
  toFun := fun V => ∑ s ∈ support V, if Multiset.map toIrrep s = i then coeff s V else 0

And terms with a given mass dimension by 

def massDimCoeff (n : ℚ) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential where
  toFun := fun V => ∑ s ∈ support V, if (s.map massDimension).sum = n then coeff s V else 0

We can then write things down as follows: 

lemma irrepCoeff_ψ_barψ_eq_zero_of_isInvariant {V : EffectivePotential} (hV : IsInvariant V) :
    irrepCoeff {Irrep.ψ, Irrep.barψ} V = 0 := by
  sorry

Which basically splits the calculation of the invariance of an effective potential and its form into a calculation of what its projection looks like in one of these irreducible representation spaces. This means we can make quite general statements about any effective potential and its terms within a given space. These spaces don't have too high a dimension and therefore should be relatively easy to prove things about generally.

Regarding the terminology in the codebase, I wanted to suggest that we might want to reconsider using the term "effective potential" for what we are building, as it might cause some confusion for incoming physicists. In standard QFT, the effective potential (such as the Coleman-Weinberg potential) specifically refers to the Legendre transform of the generating functional. It is an inherently quantum concept used to evaluate the exact vacuum structure of a theory by incorporating all quantum loop corrections (1PI diagrams).

However, what we are formalizing here is purely structural and algebraic. We are constructing the space of all possible non-derivative interaction terms—like the classical scalar potential, the Yukawa sector, and mass terms—up to mass-dimension 4 that are allowed by Lorentz and gauge symmetries.

Because of this, it might be much clearer to align our naming conventions with SMEFT (Standard Model Effective Field Theory). What we are essentially doing is mathematically classifying the operator basis for an effective Lagrangian. Referring to this structure as an "EFT operator basis" or the "non-derivative effective Lagrangian" would be much more precise. It accurately reflects the model-building and invariant theory we are formalizing, while avoiding the implication of loop-corrected quantum potentials.

I spent some time reviewing the whole background, and I'd like to check my understanding — please correct me where it's off.

My picture is that mathematical gauge theory splits into two halves. The algebraic half — Lie groups, representations, duals/conjugates, invariant theory — is what we have been building all along (the particle reps, LagrangianTheory, etc.), and there we follow the mathematical treatment exactly.   • Jet gauge group is not an approximation: it is exactly the local gauge data needed
    • Captures gauge function value and all derivatives at a point (Taylor series structure)
    • Full gauge group action factors through the jet gauge group action

Free Derivative vs. Jet Algebra

  • Free derivative was always an approximation: assumed co-variant derivatives without commutation
    • Required adding commutation rules and Jacobi identity by hand
    • Was never a jet bundle because jet bundles explicitly enforce commutation
  • Jet algebra subsumes free derivative: the old algebra maps cleanly into the new one
  • Lagrangian must live in an algebra (not evaluated on fields directly)
    • Fermions evaluated on fields reduce to complex numbers, losing structure
    • Jet algebra is the correct object: polynomial Lagrangians are the only assumption

Two Core Theorems to Prove

  • Theorem 1: if a Lagrangian is gauge invariant, it can be written in terms of field strengths and covariant derivatives
    • Already proved for single gauge boson (U1, abelian case), fully generally without mass dimension restriction
    • Goal: generalize to gluons (SU3) and then to the full Standard Model
  • Theorem 2: explicit construction of all terms that can appear in the Lagrangian (up to mass dimension)
    • Proved for QED: kinetic term for gauge boson, kinetic term for fermion, interaction term
    • Not needed for SU3 yet; focus there is Theorem 1 first
  • Non-abelian caveat: only one direction of Theorem 1 holds for SU3
    • Forward direction (gauge invariant → in field strength algebra) is true
    • Backward direction is false: gauge group acts on field strength in non-abelian case
    • Abelian case is misleadingly forgiving; both directions happen to hold there

Approach to Non-Abelian Proof (SU3)

  • Key insight: in non-abelian case, gauge transformation of A contains a Maurer-Cartan form term plus a commutator
    • Abelian: commutator vanishes, only Maurer-Cartan form survives
    • Non-abelian: need to construct a sequence of gauge transformations to isolate the right structure
  • Proposed strategy: act first with full transformation g, then with constant g₀
    • g₀ evaluated at a point is constant; second action knocks out the first term
    • Result: A transforms like the abelian case via two composed transformations
  • AI well-suited to finding the correct sequence of transformations
    • Analogous to how it solved the U1 case: chose g to pick out derivatives of Maurer-Cartan form, then used translation action on algebra
  • SU3 results already generated (from AI run before the call):
    • SU3 conjugation preserves matrix trace
    • SU3 Maurer-Cartan form is traceless
    • Trace part of gluon field unchanged by full jet gauge action
    • Every jet gauge transformation factors into a base transformation and a constant transformation
    • Non-abelian derivative contains a field-dependent commutator
    • Global SU3 transformation confirms covariance, not invariance

QED Formalization Plan

  • QED is the milestone: only truly successful quantum field theory, so proving it is significant
  • Current state: boson done, electron done; covariant derivative only done for boson, not for conjugate fermion
  • Two directions for QED:
    • Internal: formalize gauge boson part, connect to electromagnetic theory
    • External: rest of Standard Model work builds on QED as baseline
  • Connecting QED to electromagnetism

    • Plan: use the vector potential from the electromagnetism file in Mathlib
    • Electromagnetism sits at the intersection of SU2 and U1; boson defined as linear combination of W bosons
    • Should be straightforward since it is abelian; bridge should be easy to make

Mass Dimension and Open Problems

  • Mass dimension not yet handled in the new jet algebra setup
    • Previously not needed for purely fermionic case
    • Now required: infinite number of derivatives means mass dimension must constrain terms
  • Likely carries over from prior work: principle behind mass dimension should transfer
    • Derivatives just shift mass dimension of the object; concept unchanged
  • Covariant derivatives of field strength: normal derivatives in non-abelian case, covariant in abelian case (to be confirmed)
  • Total derivatives: quotienting by them should be straightforward once main theorem is proved

I think the key way to sum things out with the new invariance proof is that:

  1. Invariance under the full Lorentz group only requires invariance under boosts along the three axis x, y and z.
  2. Boosts in e.g. the zzz direction define a grading on JetAlgebra via their eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Those members of the graded submodule kkk transform as ρk\rho^kρk under a boost with rapidity ρ\rhoρ. This grading is what we call boost weight
  3. The elements of JetAlgebra which are invariant under boosts in the zzz-direction are in the 000 th submodule of this grading.
  4. The intersection of the 000 th submodules in the xxx, yyy and zzz th directions give us those elements of JetAlgebra which are fully invariant under the Lorentz group.

I think the following is a better definition of TransformsAsUnder 

/-- The `p`-th derivative at the base point of a jet: the Taylor coefficient
  scaled by the multiplicities' factorials. -/
noncomputable def jetCoeff (p : Multiset (Fin 1 ⊕ Fin 3)) (φ : JetRing) : ℂ :=
  (∏ μ, (p.count μ)! : ℕ) • MvPowerSeries.coeff p.toFinsupp φ

/-- The family of generators `f`, indexed by a derivative multi-index and a
  component index `ι`, transforms under `rep` as a field in the representation
  `ρJ` together with all its derivatives: the all-orders Leibniz rule, where each
  splitting `s = p + q` of the derivative multi-index contributes the `p`-th
  derivative of the representation matrix against the `q`-th derivative
  generator. -/
def TransformsAsUnder {B : Type} [Ring B] [Algebra ℂ B]
    (rep : Representation ℂ JetGaugeGroupI B)
    (ρJ : JetGaugeGroupI → Matrix ι ι JetRing)
    (f : Multiset (Fin 1 ⊕ Fin 3) → ι → B) : Prop :=
  ∀ U s i, rep U (f s i) =
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun pq => ∑ a, jetCoeff pq.1 (ρJ U i a) • f pq.2 a).sum
